summary: Describes how the ITU-T and the ISOC and IETF collaborate on standards work. It sets out the process for the two organizations to coordinate. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 3356.

eli5.summary: Two big groups that write rules for communication agreed on how to work together so they do not make clashing rules.

subtitle: The framework for joint standards work between the Internet Engineering Task Force and the International Telecommunication Union.

tldr.problem: The rapid growth of the Internet created overlapping work in IP-based networks between the IETF (which standardizes Internet protocols) and the ITU-T (which standardizes telecommunications), requiring coordination to avoid conflicts and duplication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2436 documents a collaboration process with designated contact points between the organizations, procedures for learning about each other's work items, representation at each other's meetings, shared mailing lists, and guidelines for referencing documents from one organization in the other's standards.
tldr.outcome: The process enabled the IETF and ITU-T to coordinate standards development, allowing both organizations to contribute their expertise to common areas like signaling, routing, security, and access.

facts.label: Contact levels
facts.value: Two: high-level strategic and working-level tactical

today: RFC 2436 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 3356, which provides updated guidance on collaboration as both organizations evolved.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
RFC 2436 describes the collaboration process between the International Telecommunication Union Standardization Sector (ITU-T) and the Internet Society (ISOC) and Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). As the Internet and IP-based networks became central to telecommunications, many work topics overlapped between the two organizations. The ITU-T, which has roots in traditional telephone networks, began addressing IP-based systems. The IETF, founded to standardize Internet protocols, found its work increasingly relevant to telecommunications operators and equipment manufacturers.

The document was created at the ITU-T TSAG (Telecommunication Standardization Advisory Group) meeting in September 1998. It recognizes that although collaboration already existed in some areas, it needed to be strengthened and formalized. The RFC details processes for mutual awareness, representation, communication, and document sharing to ensure both organizations can draw on each other's competence and experience effectively.
sections.eli5: The Internet group (IETF) and the telephone standards group (ITU-T) realized they were both writing rules about the same things. They decided to agree on how to work together so they did not conflict.

sections.title: Collaboration Framework and Representation
sections.content:
The collaboration model rests on mutual recognition and formal representation. ISOC and the IETF have been admitted by the ITU Council to participate in ITU-T work, giving ISOC delegates equivalent rights to other ITU-T Study Group participants. Conversely, ITU-T members may participate in IETF work as individuals or as recognized ITU-T delegates. The RFC emphasizes that IETF participants may attend ITU-T meetings as ISOC delegates if their IETF Working Group has approved attendance, and that ITU-T Study Group Chairmen can authorize official delegates to represent them at IETF meetings.

The framework establishes two levels of contact points: high-level (ITU-T Study Group Chairman with IETF Area Director) for long-term strategic coordination, and working level (ITU-T Rapporteur with IETF Working Group Chair) for day-to-day collaboration. Communication between contact points can be informal, but formal positions must be explicitly approved. Mailing list subscription is encouraged: IETF experts should participate in IETF Working Group lists (the primary forum for IETF discussion), while IETF participants may join ITU-T formal mailing lists if affiliated with an ITU-T member (ISOC can designate representatives).
sections.eli5: The groups set up named contact people at different levels so messages get to the right desk. They agreed that experts from one group could sit in on the other's meetings and participate in their discussions.

sections.title: Discovering Overlapping Work and Coordination
sections.content:
A central mechanism for identifying potential collaboration is for each organization to monitor the other's work items. ITU-T Study Groups are encouraged to review current IETF Working Groups to identify topics of mutual interest (details are in IETF charters). When a Study Group finds overlap, it should contact both the IETF Working Group Chair and the relevant IETF Area Director. The IETF maintains a mailing list for proposed new Working Group charters, open by subscription; it is recommended that Study Group Chairmen (or delegates) subscribe to spot new work of interest. The IETF turnaround time for new charters is one week, so active monitoring is needed. Feedback on charters should be sent to the IESG mailing list, clearly marked as an ITU-T position.

Conversely, the ITU-T provides initial information on Internet-related topics in its Study Groups to the ISOC Vice President of Standards, who distributes it to interested IETF individuals. Study Groups are asked to send updates as they arise, and any IETF Working Group interest is forwarded to relevant Study Group Chairmen. When collaboration is identified, the Study Group should describe it in its work plan, noting the goal and expected outcome.
sections.eli5: Each group looks at what the other group is doing. When they spot work on the same topic, they let each other know and decide if they should work together.

sections.title: Document Sharing and Cross-Referencing
sections.content:
During collaboration, organizations share working drafts and specifications. Initial concepts are typically circulated by email, repeating the concept without full details. More formally, IETF Internet Drafts can be submitted to an ITU-T Study Group as a Contribution from ISOC if the IETF Working Group agrees there is mutual benefit. The ISOC Vice President of Standards reviews and approves, then forwards to the ITU-T Technical Standards Bureau (TSB) for distribution as a Study Group Contribution. Conversely, ITU-T draft Recommendations can be sent as Internet Drafts to the IETF (which are temporary documents expiring six months after publication) if the Study Group decides there is benefit. The document editor is instructed to prepare it in Internet Draft format, and submit to the Internet Draft editor, or post to a website with a short Internet Draft containing a summary and URL.

The RFC strongly discourages joint or common text between the organizations because of differences in approval, revision, and stability processes. Instead, the preferred outcome is for one body to fully document a topic and the other to reference it (described in section 3.4). Both the Rapporteur and Document Editor should be identified as contacts, and the Internet Draft must clearly state that it is a working document of a particular ITU-T Study Group.
sections.eli5: When one group writes something useful, the other can take it and comment on it, or include it in their own work by referencing it. But they do not try to write rules together because their approval processes are too different.

sections.title: Standards Cross-Referencing and Approval Guidelines
sections.content:
ITU-T Recommendation A.5 describes how to reference IETF RFCs in ITU-T Recommendations, and IETF RFC 2026 (section 7.1.1) describes how to reference other standards like ITU-T Recommendations in IETF RFCs. The RFC includes application guidelines developed at ITU-T TSAG meetings to address practical issues: references should be to specific versions of standards (giving ITU-T control of what is referenced), referenced standards should remain publicly available, and when a draft Recommendation references another organization's standard, the TSB should notify that organization of impending changes.

The guidelines address complex scenarios such as nested references (when one RFC references another RFC that references an ITU-T Recommendation). In such cases, all references within the RFC should be listed in the Study Group's decision report. For Informational and Experimental RFCs, or Historic RFCs, normative referencing is generally not appropriate. Proposed Standards may be referenced with caution, on a case-by-case basis, since they may change. Finally, references should ideally be freely available via the Web so purchasers of one standard can access the referenced documents.
sections.eli5: Both groups follow rules about how to refer to the other group's documents. They do not directly copy, just point to the other document. If the document is updated, they have to decide if they need to change their own work.
